subtype: Approach: identifying what voters actually need [Thinking]
passage: Akash sat with a blank page headed Manifesto and realised he had only "better school, better future." That meant nothing. So he decided to ask. During recess, with a notebook and one question, "What one thing would you fix?", he went from bench to bench. Canteen queues, said Aadhya; her Class 9 friends waited twenty minutes for one samosa. The football club had two working balls. The library closed at four, before club practice ended. By Friday he had ninety-one answers in tally marks, and three problems came up again and again. Akash crossed out the vague lines and wrote three: a second canteen counter, more balls, library open until five. "Now I can promise something specific," he said, "and people can check it."

qa.q: How many answers did Akash collect by Friday?
What did Akash realise about the first draft of the manifesto, and how did he feel?
qa.a: Akash realised 'better school, better future' meant nothing, and felt dissatisfied enough to go and ask classmates.

qa.q: What other approach could Akash use to check the ideas, and why?
qa.a: Akash could talk to the principal and canteen staff about what is possible, because a promise voters can check needs to be one that can be kept.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see the campaign question?
qa.a: Aadhya likely feels listened to, since a real complaint about the canteen queue was asked for and could turn into a promise.

grounding: A candidate for school captain asks classmates about canteen queues, sports equipment and library hours, and builds a platform on concrete issues instead of general promises of change.

passage:
"Your speech says 'I will bring change'," Manoj said, reading Chinmay's draft on the canteen bench. "Change to what?"

"Everything. The school needs it."

"Everyone says that. Did you ask anyone what they want?"

Chinmay was quiet. Then: "Okay. Let's ask."

At break he went table to table. "What's one thing that annoys you here?"

"The canteen line," said a Class 8 girl. "Twenty minutes, then the bell."

"No footballs that aren't flat," said a boy.

"Library shuts at two," said someone from Class 12. "We have free periods at three."

Back on the bench, Chinmay crossed out 'change'. "So it's three things. Two canteen counters at break. Pump and replace footballs each term. Ask if the library can stay open till four." He looked up. "These I can actually argue for."

Manoj grinned. "Now it sounds like you listened."

qa.q: How long did the Class 8 girl say the canteen line took?
qa.a: She said it took twenty minutes, then the bell rang.

qa.q: What does Chinmay's silence after Manoj's question suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt caught out and a bit embarrassed, realising he had not asked anyone what they actually wanted.

qa.q: What else could Chinmay do to check his platform before the speech?
qa.a: He could run a quick show-of-hands poll in a few classes on his three issues, to see which matters most to most students.

qa.q: How might the students Chinmay spoke to see his campaign now?
qa.a: They may feel heard and more likely to trust him, since his promises now name the exact problems they told him about.

grounding: Shows a candidate asking classmates about everyday problems like canteen queues, sports equipment and library hours, and building a concrete platform from them.

subtype: Approach: identifying what voters actually need [Thinking]
passage:
When I decided to run for school captain last year, my first poster said, "A Better Tomorrow." Nikita, my friend from the hostel, looked at it and asked, "Better how?" I didn't have an answer, and that bothered me all night.

So I made a small notebook and spent a week asking people one question at dinner and in the corridors: what's hard here? I thought I'd hear big things. Instead I heard about the hostel water cooler that leaked, the football nets full of holes, and the reading room that closed before prep time ended.

That's when it clicked for me. Voters don't live in "tomorrow". They live in queues and broken nets.

I rewrote everything around those three fixes. I'm Siddharth, and I didn't win by much, but I won, and I remember that notebook.

qa.q: What did the first poster say?
qa.a: The first poster said, "A Better Tomorrow."

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel after Nikita asked "Better how?"
qa.a: Siddharth felt uneasy and bothered all night, because there was no real answer behind the slogan.

qa.q: What else could Siddharth have done besides the notebook?
qa.a: Siddharth could have held a short open meeting in the hostel common room, so students could build on each other's complaints and rank them.

qa.q: How might Nikita see the change in the campaign?
qa.a: Nikita would probably feel pleased and a bit proud, since one honest question pushed the campaign toward real problems.

grounding: A reflective account of a candidate asking students what is hard in daily school life and replacing vague promises with concrete fixes.
